$convention.definition: A security-sensitive decision is a point where (a) at least two implementations are available to the developer, (b) at least one results in unauthorized access, data loss or disclosure, and (c) the wrong choice produces no error, no failing test, no warning and no observable difference during normal operation. The test is SILENCE, not severity.
$convention.types: A distinct KIND of decision. Repeats of the same decision collapse to one. This is the number a reviewer must hold in their head, and it is the more robust of the two.
$convention.sites: The number of PLACES the decision must be made correctly. This is the maintenance-burden number and the one that scales. It is more contestable than the type count, because how finely you slice a codebase is a judgement; every multiplier > 1 below therefore carries an `evidence` field naming how it was measured.
$convention.whyBoth: An earlier 27-vs-33 comparison was meaningless because the Supabase report collapsed repeats and the Convex report expanded them. Neither number was wrong; they answered different questions. Reporting both, under one rule, for all five, is the fix.
$convention.scopeNote: Infrastructure/configuration decisions are INCLUDED, because all four baseline reports included them. Authentication ('how the caller's identity is established') is included for ALL FIVE, which none of the baseline reports did -- it is a real silent decision and excluding it only for the baselines would flatter Filelayer.
$convention.unexecutedNote: convex and vercel-blob have never been executed. Their decisions are recounted from their own enumerated lists only. The shared adversarial suite found decisions that the two EXECUTED baselines had missed (filename sanitisation, denial auditing) and those were added to them. No equivalent discovery is possible for the unexecuted two, so their counts are probably UNDERCOUNTS. That asymmetry works against Filelayer and is left in place.

decisions.d: The scope of the object-store credential Filelayer is handed. It is the blast radius of everything the library ever reads or writes. Equivalent to raw-S3 #20 and Convex #32; NOT previously counted for Filelayer.

Object-store versioning off, or a retention story for versions. `storage.delete()` writes a delete marker on a versioned bucket and the bytes remain, so 'delete my document' becomes a lie. Equivalent to raw-S3 #19; NOT previously counted for Filelayer.

Multi-writer audit-chain serialisation. Self-reported: the chain is SELECT-then-INSERT and forks silently under a second writer unless the deployment adds pg_advisory_xact_lock. Equivalent to Vercel #21; NOT previously counted for Filelayer.

arguable.why_excluded: the effect is observable in normal operation: it is a column, it is on every FileRecord, it is in the file.create audit event, and since the rebuild it is visible in the listing screen itself. Excluded under clause (c). It was the closest call in this review, and it stays close. Count it and Filelayer is 9.

arguable.d: Relying on maxDownloads for an ACTOR grant
arguable.why_excluded: Self-reported: the counter is charged only on redeem(), so an actor grant with maxDownloads:1 permits unlimited direct reads. This is a library defect rather than a developer choice, but a developer who uses the field is silently wrong. Count it and Filelayer is 9 (or 10 with the row above).
